newsitem.title: GERMANY: German April M3 growth to slow but miss Buba goal.
newsitem.headline: German April M3 growth to slow but miss Buba goal.

text.p: German M3 money supply growth is likely to have slowed again in April, continuing the steady downward path plotted since the beginning of this year, economists said on Wednesday.

But since growth will not fall sharply enough to bring M3 within the Bundesbank's 3.5 to 6.5 percent range -- a move unlikely to come before the end of 1997 or early 1998 -- the data will not be enough to prompt the central bank into any near-term monetary easing.

"M3 growth is still buoyant although it is decelerating somewhat," said Stefan Schneider, economist at Paribas in Frankfurt. "But so far there is certainly no reason for the Bundesbank to cut interest rates."
Schneider is forecasting an April M3 growth of 7.6 percent.

The average of forecasts from economists polled by Reuters is for an annualised, seasonally-adjusted 7.7 percent growth rate in April versus 8.3 percent in March -- still substantially above the Bundesbank's target range.
Growth in M3, which is seen as an early indicator of inflationary pressure, has fallen from 11.7 percent in January, to 9.1 percent in February and then to 8.3 percent in March.
Petra Koehler, an economist at Dresdner Bank in Frankfurt, expects a sharp decline in April, forecasting a 6.8 percent rate versus 8.3 percent in March.

With public insecurity growing about possible changes in social and tax systems, analysts said capital formation, which had declined in the early part of 1997, was expected to have picked up again in April.
Capital formation slows M3 money supply growth since it drains funds from areas included in the M3 definition of money supply.

Hans-Juergen Meltzer, economist at Deutsche Bank Research in Frankfurt said these factors, coupled with higher unemployment which add to public worries, will boost capital formation and contribute to a slowdown in M3 growth.
Meltzer expects M3 to slow to 7.8 percent in April, slightly above consensus forecast.
An added braking factor will be lower borrowing needs from federal and local government bodies, analysts said.
Koehler said that due to very weak tax revenues in the early part of this year, loan requirements from these offices had been particularly high, but should drop slightly for April.

But like other analysts, Koehler said that money supply data has lost its decisive role as a German monetary indicator and the Bundesbank is widely expected to leave interest rates on hold for the medium term.
"M3 does not carry such a high priority as it did before," said Schneider.

"The Bundesbank made it quite clear in one of its recent reports that it also takes other indicators into account, so I don't think that any kind of rate movement in the next six months would be strongly based on M3 numbers," he said.
